title: POC Weekly Caching Sync - Prefix/KV hit rates & prompt reuse
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on caching metrics (prefix vs KV cache), prompt reuse opportunities, and next steps for improving hit rates. Redwood SE reviewed recent benchmark runs, highlighted cold-start behavior for chat sessions, and proposed key normalization and TTL tuning. Customer raised security and data-retention questions for cached prefixes and asked for an updated runbook and benchmark CSV. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share updated caching runbook, run a dedicated latency benchmark with adjusted keys, and schedule a follow-up check-in.
topics: KV cache behavior for multi-turn chat
Prompt reuse strategy and key normalization
action_items: Priya Singh - Share annotated benchmark CSV with per-model hit rates by 2026-04-16
Alex Martinez - Send updated caching runbook + example key-normalization code by 2026-04-17

transcript:
Header: Date: 2026-04-14 13:00 PDT | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Alex Martinez (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Acme Eng Manager), Samira Khan (Acme ML Eng), Tom Nguyen (Acme Infra)

Auto-summary: quick run-through of last week's changes and new benchmark results. Some minor transcription errors expected (k-v cash, V P C sometimes).

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:07] Jordan: Jordan Lee here.
[00:09] Samira: Samira - hi.
[00:11] Tom: Tom here.
[00:13] Priya: Priya from Redwood. Alex?
[00:15] Alex: Alex here. Alright let's jump in. Priya you ran the caching jobs this week?
[00:23] Priya: Yep, I re-ran the prefix + KV cache experiments against the latest prompt families Samira gave. The high level: prefix cache hit rate improved from ~18% to ~31% on the text-gen workloads after key normalization. KV cache for multi-turn chat is still low, about 12% overall, but for the reused session patterns it's up to low 40s.
[00:40] Jordan: 12% feels low — what's causing misses?
[00:43] Priya: A few things: inconsistent punctuation and variable user metadata in prefixes, plus TTLs expiring between turns for longer sessions. Also our key hashing was sensitive to whitespace differences, so normalizing whitespace and lowercasing helped.
[01:00] Samira: Can you explain the difference again between prefix cache and KV cache in our setup? I think some folks here still conflate them.
[01:08] Priya: Sure — prefix cache is matching the earlier tokens of the prompt to serve cached logits/embeddings; KV cache is the attention key-value cache for autoregressive decoding across tokens. Prefix is great for repeated prompts, KV helps across turns when the conversation reuses context.
[01:26] Tom: Are we observing any memory pressure with higher KV reuse? We run several models on our dedicated pool.
[01:31] Priya: Not yet at the POC scale, but if we skewer the sequence lengths up it'll increase KV memory usage. We measured per-session KV growth in the run. I'll share the CSV.
[01:43] Alex: Quick question on latency — did enabling prefix cache change p95 numbers?
[01:47] Priya: Yes, median token latency dropped about 18% when the prefix hit; p95 improved marginally — because cold starts still dominate for some request patterns. The dataset we used has a long tail of unique prompts.
[02:02] Jordan: Do you have the absolute numbers? Our SLO is 350ms p95 for short completions.
[02:06] Priya: For the short workload runs: cold p95 was ~520ms, warm (prefix hit) p95 was ~320ms. So when hit rate increases we get under 350ms frequently.
[02:19] Samira: That's promising. What's the biggest lever to get prefix hit rate beyond 31%?
[02:23] Priya: Key normalizing, grouping prompts into families (we used fuzzy matching thresholds), and introducing a short-term LRU for near-duplicate prompts. Also encouraging prompt reuse on client side (templating) helps a ton.
[02:37] Jordan: About client-side templating — can you show example?
[02:40] Alex: We'll send examples in the runbook. Priya has a snippet that strips variable tokens and replaces with placeholders.
[02:47] Priya: Right, e.g., replace user names, timestamps with placeholders before hashing the key so similar prompts map to same prefix entry.
[02:55] Tom: Any implications for data privacy if we normalize and cache?
[02:59] Priya: Our recommendation: don't cache PII fields; tokenization/placeholder step should strip or mask PII. Also store only encrypted cache entries and rotate KMS keys per compliance. We touched on this in last week's security doc.
[03:13] Jordan: Good. On TTLs — what's the tradeoff you recommend?
[03:16] Priya: Short TTLs (30–120s) for high-turn systems to avoid staleness; longer TTLs (5–15m) for stable prompts. It depends on workload. The run had a 2m default TTL which caused some multi-turn misses.
[03:32] Samira: How about cross-model caching? We use small variant orchard models for cost savings — can cached prefixes be reused across quantized/variant models?
[03:40] Priya: You can reuse cached embeddings or logits only if the models are compatible. For different architecture or quantization noise, hit quality degrades. Better approach: cache at a normalized representation (e.g., embedding) and check a compatibility table. We'll include per-model compatibility in the runbook.
[03:59] Alex: Are there any numbers on cost impact?
[04:01] Priya: Rough estimate: each prefix hit avoided ~0.35 tokens of generation work and ~0.25 GPU-ms; translating to approx 8–12% cost reduction on the workloads that had 31% hit. Exact numbers in CSV.
[04:16] Jordan: Competitors like Vertex and Anthropic claim different caching approaches; did you benchmark against them?
[04:22] Priya: We didn't run third-party endpoints in this POC due to legal reasons, but we compared conceptual approaches — we noted Vertex has server-side caching but less prefix normalization, Anthropic's tooling is more integrated; we can run side-by-side if you want but it will take extra time and approvals.
[04:39] Tom: Security folks will want to see audit logs for cache access. Do you provide that?
[04:43] Alex: Yes — Redwood's private and dedicated modes provide cache access logs + audit trails. We'll share the SOC2 notes.
[04:50] Samira: Earlier you said KV cache hit was 12% overall but 40% for reused patterns — can you explain the skew?
[04:58] Priya: The 12% is session-agnostic: many sessions are unique or have short turns. For a subset of users who reuse templates or have repeated flows, KV reuse is higher. The distribution is heavy-tailed.
[05:12] Jordan: For our pilot, what's the recommended client changes?
[05:15] Alex: Minimal: implement the placeholder templating, send a cache-key hint in the request metadata, and sample telemetry for a week. That should lift prefix hits.
[05:25] Samira: We can do templating. We'll need examples for our node-based backend.
[05:29] Priya: I'll include node/py snippets in the runbook; Alex will send the runbook link.
[05:36] Jordan: About the benchmark — you mentioned a 1k request run for p95?
[05:40] Priya: That's right. We'll run 1k short completions and measure cold vs warm, plus a chat workload with 200 sessions to measure KV behavior.
[05:50] Tom: What about autoscaling interactions? If cache hit reduces load, autoscaler might scale down and then re-scale causing weirdness.
[05:58] Priya: Good point — autoscaler window needs to account for reduced token generation. For Dedicated pools we recommend a slightly higher baseline or a burst policy to avoid oscillation. We'll document policies.
[06:11] Jordan: Any follow-up on latency tests in VPC/dedicated mode vs hosted? We care about p95 in our VPC.
[06:18] Priya: Our previous runs showed VPC adds a ~30–60ms network overhead; dedicated pools can reduce queuing. We'll run the dedicated benchmark once your infra peering is set.
[06:30] Tom: I'll confirm peering schedule after the meeting.
[06:33] Samira: On prompt families — we've attached two sample families. In production there are more.
[06:38] Priya: Great — Samira, can you confirm those families are representative?
[06:41] Samira: Yes, they're 70% of our short-completion traffic.
[06:45] Alex: Cool. Any blockers?
[06:48] Jordan: Only internal security review pending but we can proceed with non-prod tests.
[06:53] Priya: I'll run the benchmark tomorrow and share the CSV; expect the annotated sheet by Friday.
[06:58] Alex: Let's talk about key normalization detail — Priya, run through the code quickly?
[07:02] Priya: Sure — we trim whitespace, lowercase, replace number-like tokens and emails with placeholders, collapse repeated whitespace, and optionally hash the normalized string with a stable hash. Here's a quick pseudo example... (code noise)
[07:22] Samira: What about user language differences? We have multi-lingual prompts.
[07:26] Priya: Language-specific tokenization matters. Normalization rules should be per-language; for some languages lowercasing isn't valid. We'll add language-aware rules to the runbook.
[07:38] Jordan: Any expected regressions in output quality if we over-normalize?
[07:42] Priya: Potentially — if placeholders remove semantic distinctions. We recommend a conservative normalization threshold and running quality regressions on a labeled eval set.
[07:53] Samira: Can Redwood tie cache misses to specific prompt examples for debugging?
[07:57] Priya: Yes, we can provide sampled trace logs that map request -> computed key -> cache outcome. Those logs are redactable for PII.
[08:07] Tom: On the encryption piece, how often do you rotate KMS keys?
[08:10] Alex: Depends on enterprise policy, but we support key rotation and HSM-backed keys. Security team can request details; we'll share the compliance packet.
[08:20] Jordan: Okay, let's recap next steps.
[08:24] Alex: Priya will share benchmark CSV + annotated notes by Friday. I'll send the runbook with code snippets. Samira will provide additional prompt families. Tom to confirm VPC peering schedule. We'll reconvene next week.
[08:36] Jordan: That works. Anything else?
[08:38] Samira: One ask — can you include an example of TTL vs hit-rate tradeoff in the runbook?
[08:42] Priya: Yes, there's a chart in draft form; I'll include numbers from our run.
[08:46] Alex: Great. Thanks everyone.
[08:48] Jordan: Thanks.
[08:49] Meeting end.

Notes: Some timestamps are approximate; occasional words mis-transcribed (k-v cash, V P C). Attachments mentioned: runbook link (to be sent), benchmark CSV (to be shared).
